lessons.title: Plasma Cutting: Techniques and Safety
lessons.body:
Plasma cutting is the fastest way to slice through steel up to 25mm thick. In Africa, where oxy-acetylene can be expensive and hard to refill, a plasma cutter running on a 220V generator is a game-changer. You need a plasma cutter rated for at least 40 amps, a clean dry air supply (moisture traps are essential in humid coastal areas), and a face shield with shade #8 or darker. Never cut without leather gloves, a leather apron, and closed shoes. Sparks fly at 1500Â°C and will burn through synthetic clothing.

Before cutting, clean the metal with a wire brush to remove rust, paint, and oil. Set your amperage based on thickness: 30A for 6mm, 40A for 10mm, 60A for 15mm. For a clean cut, maintain a 1.5â3mm standoff between the tip and the metal. Drag the tip lightly if you have a drag shield, or use a standoff guide. Start the cut at the edge, not in the middle, unless you are piercing. To pierce, tilt the torch 30Â° to blow molten metal away, then straighten once through.

Move at a steady speedâtoo fast leaves dross (recast metal) on the bottom, too slow creates a wide kerf and excessive dross. Listen to the sound: a steady hiss means good speed. If you see sparks spraying upward, you are too slow. Practice on scrap 6mm plate: draw straight lines, circles, and curves. In many African workshops, plasma cutters are used to cut decorative panels, gates, and sculpture components. Keep a bucket of water nearby to quench hot cuts and reduce fire risk.

Maintenance: drain your air compressor daily, replace the consumables (electrode, nozzle, swirl ring) when the cut quality drops. A worn nozzle gives a ragged edge. Store consumables in a dry place. If you are using a generator, ensure it delivers clean powerâvoltage spikes kill plasma cutters. Always cut in a well-ventilated area, as plasma cutting produces fumes, especially on galvanized or painted steel. Wear a respirator if cutting coated metals.

lessons.title: Angle Grinding and Cutting
lessons.body:
An angle grinder is the most versatile tool in a metal sculptorâs kit. In Africa, the 115mm (4.5-inch) grinder is common, but for fabrication, a 230mm (9-inch) grinder is better for cutting thick steel. Always use the correct disc: a cutting disc for slicing, a grinding disc for smoothing, and a flap disc for finishing. Never use a cutting disc for grindingâit can shatter. Check the discâs maximum RPM; it must be higher than the grinderâs no-load RPM (usually 11,000 for 115mm, 6,500 for 230mm).

Safety first: wear safety glasses or a face shield, ear plugs, and leather gloves. Tie back long hair and remove loose clothing. The grinder can kick back if the disc bindsâhold it firmly with two hands, and position yourself so the grinder is not in line with your body. For cutting, let the disc do the work; donât force it. Use a metal straight edge or a scribed line as a guide. For clean cuts, score the line with a cut-off wheel, then cut in one smooth motion. If cutting sheet metal, sandwich it between plywood to reduce vibration.

Grinding: hold the grinder at a 15â30Â° angle to the work. Move side to side to avoid gouging. For weld preparation, grind a 30Â° bevel on each plate for a V-groove. For finishing, use a 60â80 grit flap disc to blend welds, then a 120 grit for a smoother finish. In many African workshops, youâll use a grinder to clean up welds, remove rust, and shape metal. Keep a fire extinguisher nearbyâgrinding sparks can ignite sawdust or rags.

Maintenance: unplug the grinder before changing discs. Use the spanner to tighten the discânever hand-tighten. Check the power cord for damage. Replace worn brushes. Store grinders in a dry place. If you are using a generator, ensure it can handle the grinderâs starting surge (usually 2â3 times running watts). A 2.2kW generator will run a 115mm grinder but struggle with a 230mm. Always let the grinder spin down before setting it down.

lessons.title: Bending with a Brake and Roller
lessons.body:
Bending metal opens up a world of formsâfrom curved sculpture panels to structural brackets. A brake (press brake or box-and-pan brake) makes straight bends; a roller (slip roller) makes curves. In Africa, many workshops build their own brakes from heavy channel iron and hinges. For a manual brake, you need a bed, a clamping bar, and a bending apron. The thickness capacity depends on the brakeâs size: a 1.2m brake can bend 1.5mm sheet, while a 2.4m brake can bend 1mm. Always check the brakeâs ratingânever exceed it.

To bend on a brake: mark your bend line with a scribe or soapstone. Set the back gauge for the distance from the bend to the edge. Clamp the sheet between the bed and clamping bar, aligning the bend line with the front edge of the bed. Lift the apron handles smoothlyâjerking causes cracks. For a 90Â° bend, you may need to overbend slightly (2â3Â°) to account for springback. For a radius bend, use a radius bar or a piece of pipe clamped in the brake. Practice on scrap: bend a 100mm wide strip to 90Â°, then measure the inside radius.

A slip roller has three rolls: one top roll and two bottom rolls. The gap between rolls determines the curve radius. To roll a cylinder, start with the sheet flat, lower the top roll to just touch the metal, then pass the sheet through. Tighten the top roll a quarter turn each pass until you reach the desired radius. For a cone, you need a slip roller with a cone attachment or you can hand-form over a pipe. In many African metal shops, rollers are used to make rings, curved gates, and sculpture bases. Always feed the metal squarelyâif it goes in crooked, it will come out crooked.

Safety: wear gloves when handling sheet metalâedges are sharp. Keep fingers clear of the rolls. For the brake, never put your hands between the clamping bar and the bed. Maintenance: oil the pivot points and gears regularly. Check for cracks in the bending apron. Store brake and roller under a cover to prevent rust. If you donât have a brake, you can bend metal in a vise with a hammer and a block of wood, but for repeatable bends, a brake is essential.

lessons.title: Advanced Welding: Vertical and Overhead
lessons.body:
Vertical and overhead welding are the tests that separate a hobbyist from a professional. In Africa, these positions are common when building gates, roofs, and sculptures that cannot be rotated. For vertical welding, you can weld uphill or downhill. Uphill (vertical-up) gives deeper penetration and is used for structural joints; downhill is faster but weaker. For overhead, you must fight gravityâmolten metal wants to drip. The key is to use a slightly lower amperage (about 10â15% less than flat) and a shorter arc.

For vertical-up with 7018 electrode (3.2mm), set your welder to about 110â120 amps. Hold the electrode at a slight upward angle (5â15Â°). Use a triangle motion: pause at the sides, move quickly across the center. This gives a clean bead without undercut. For vertical-down with 6013 or 6011, use 90â100 amps and a straight drag motionâno weaving. Downhill is good for thin metal (up to 6mm) but not for thick sections.

Overhead welding: use 6011 or 7018 (3.2mm) at 100â115 amps. Keep the arc shortâabout the diameter of the electrode core. Use a back-and-forth motion or a small circle. The puddle must be small and cool quickly. If the puddle gets too large, it will drip. Tilt the electrode slightly in the direction of travel. For a fillet weld overhead, aim the electrode at the root of the joint, then push slightly into the corner. Practice on scrap plates clamped overheadâstart with a T-joint. In many African workshops, overhead welding is needed for repairing truck frames or building carports.

Safety: wear a leather welding jacket, gloves, and a welding cap. Use a welding screen to protect others from arc flash. Ensure good ventilationâwelding fumes rise, so an overhead weld puts your face right in the plume. Use a respirator if welding galvanized or painted steel. Keep a fire watcher nearby if welding near flammable materials. Maintenance: check your electrode holder and ground clamp for tight connections. Replace worn cables. Clean spatter from your helmet lens. Practice makes perfectâspend at least 20 hours on each position before calling yourself competent.

lessons.title: Jigs and Fixtures for Repetition
lessons.body:
If you need to make 50 identical brackets, a jig saves time and ensures accuracy. A jig holds the workpiece; a fixture holds the tool. In African metal shops, jigs are often made from scrap steel, bolts, and clamps. Start simple: for a repeated cut, weld a stop block to your cutting table. For drilling, make a drill jig from a piece of flat bar with hardened drill bushings. For welding, a fixture table with slots and clamps is ideal, but you can build a simple jig from angle iron and toggle clamps.

Example: making a hundred 100x100mm angle brackets from 50x50x5mm angle iron. Build a jig: a base plate with two stopsâone for the length, one for the width. Weld a vertical post to hold the angle iron upright. Use a toggle clamp to hold the piece. Then you can drill two 10mm holes in each bracket without measuring. For welding, a jig with copper backing bars helps dissipate heat and prevents distortion. In many African workshops, jigs are used for making window frames, gates, and sculpture armatures.

Design rules: make jigs from sturdy material (at least 6mm plate or 50x50 angle). Use hardened pins for locating holes. Allow for clearanceâ0.5mm is enough for most fits. Make jigs adjustable if you need variations. Label your jigs and store them properly. For repetitive cutting, a stop on your chop saw or band saw is a simple jig. For bending, a back gauge on a brake is a jig. For assembly, a fixture table with a grid of holes (like a welding table) lets you clamp parts at precise angles.

Safety: never modify a jig while itâs in use. Use clamps that can handle the forceâa toggle clamp may slip under heavy welding. Keep jigs cleanâspatter buildup causes misalignment. Maintenance: check for wear on locating pins and stops. Replace worn parts. In Africa, where labor is often cheap but time is valuable, a good jig pays for itself in a day. If you are making multiple copies of a sculpture, a jig for the armature ensures each piece is identical. Start with a simple jig for your most repetitive task.

lessons.title: Project: Fabricated Steel Structure
lessons.body:
For this project, you will build a small steel structureâa garden bench or a display plinthâusing the skills from this module. The design: a bench 1.2m long, 0.45m wide, 0.45m high, made from 25x25x3mm square tubing and 20x3mm flat bar. You will cut, bend, weld, and finish it. This project uses plasma cutting for the seat slats, angle grinding for cleanup, bending for the legs, and vertical/overhead welding for the joints. You will also make a simple jig for the leg assemblies.

Step 1: Cut list. From 25x25x3mm tubing: 4 legs at 0.45m, 2 long rails at 1.2m, 2 short rails at 0.45m. From 20x3mm flat bar: 8 seat slats at 1.2m. Step 2: Cut all pieces with a plasma cutter or angle grinder. Clean edges with a grinder. Step 3: Bend the legs. Each leg needs a 90Â° bend at the top to form a foot. Use a brake or bend in a vise with a hammer. Step 4: Build a jig for the leg assembly: a flat plate with stops for the two legs and the short rail. Weld the legs to the short rail in the jig. Step 5: Assemble the frame: weld the long rails to the leg assemblies. Use vertical-up welding for the vertical joints and overhead for the underside. Step 6: Weld the seat slats to the frame, spacing them 10mm apart. Step 7: Grind all welds smooth. Step 8: Finish with a wire brush and paint with red oxide primer, then a top coat.

Safety: wear all PPEâwelding helmet, gloves, apron, and boots. Use clamps to hold partsânever your hands. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Work on a clean, dry surface. In Africa, this bench can be sold for $50â$100, depending on finish. You can scale the design for a table or a sculpture base. Take photos of each step for your portfolio. If you make a mistake, cut it apart and re-weldâsteel is forgiving. This project proves you can take a drawing and turn it into a functional, sellable product.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Advanced Fabrication for Metal Sculpture

This practical reference consolidates the core technical knowledge you need to move from competent welder to profitable fabricator. In the African metal sculpture market â from the roadside workshops of Accra and Nairobi to the growing art export trade in Cape Town and Dakar â the difference between a maker who earns a living and one who struggles is rarely artistic vision alone. It is the ability to produce consistent, safe, structurally sound work at a repeatable pace, with minimal material waste and maximum client confidence.

This lesson covers plasma cutting, angle grinding, bending, advanced welding positions, jigs and fixtures, and a capstone fabricated steel structure project. Treat it as your workshop manual: keep it near the bench, refer to the tables before you quote a job, and run the checklist before every fabrication session.

1. Plasma Cutting: Techniques and Safety

Plasma cutting remains the fastest way to cut sheet and plate steel up to about 25 mm in a small African workshop. A 40â60 amp inverter plasma cutter running on single-phase 220â240 V is the practical sweet spot: it handles 6â12 mm mild steel cleanly, runs off a modest generator or grid supply, and costs far less than a comparable oxy-fuel setup to operate.

Technique fundamentals: set the correct amperage for thickness, maintain a consistent standoff (typically 1.5â3 mm with a drag shield), move at a steady speed that produces a slight trailing spark angle, and pierce off the cut line before entering the profile. For sculpture work, plasma gives you the freedom to cut organic curves in 3â6 mm plate that would be slow and distorted with a grinder.

Business note: plasma consumables (electrodes, nozzles, shields) are a recurring cost. Track cuts per consumable set â a well-tuned 40 A machine should give 300â600 pierces on 6 mm steel. If you are burning through sets faster, your standoff or amperage is wrong, and you are losing money on every sculpture.

2. Angle Grinding and Cutting

The angle grinder is the most-used and most-dangerous tool in the African sculpture workshop. A 115 mm or 125 mm grinder with a 900â1400 W motor covers most tasks: cutting 3â6 mm bar and sheet, blending welds, and finishing. For heavier section work, a 230 mm grinder handles 6â9 mm cuts.

Rules that save fingers and steel: never remove the guard, always match disc RPM rating to the grinder, use the correct disc for the material (do not cut aluminium with a steel disc â loading causes kickback), and let the tool do the work. For weld dressing, a 60â80 grit flap disc gives a controllable finish; a hard grinding wheel removes metal fast but gouges if you tilt it.

Table 1: Angle grinder disc selection and application (mild steel)
Disc typeSizeBest useTypical lifeCost band (USD)
Cutting disc (flat)115â125 mmBar, tube, sheet to 6 mm20â40 cuts0.50â1.50
Cutting disc (depressed)230 mmPlate 6â9 mm, heavy section8â15 cuts2.00â4.00
Grinding wheel115â230 mmHeavy stock removal, bevel prepLong1.50â5.00
Flap disc 60â80 grit115â125 mmWeld blending, finishing1â3 mÂ²1.00â3.00
Wire cup brush115 mmRust and scale removalLong2.00â5.00

Source: 3M Abrasive Systems, Grinding and Cutting Guide (3m.com); Bosch Professional, Angle Grinder Application Manual (bosch-professional.com). Costs approximate Nairobi/Accra/Lagos wholesale, 2024.

â  SAFETY WARNING â ANGLE GRINDER KICKBACK

Never cut with the side of a cutting disc. Kickback occurs when the disc binds in the cut â the grinder can jump toward your body or hand in under a second. Always position yourself out of the kickback path, keep both hands on the tool, use the side handle, and wear a full face shield plus leather apron. Discs explode: a 125 mm disc spinning at 11,000 rpm fragments at over 200 km/h. Replace any disc that has been dropped, chipped, or run past its expiry date. In a shared African workshop, insist every operator wears eye and ear protection â hearing loss is permanent and uninsured.

3. Bending with a Brake and Roller

Clean bends separate professional sculpture from welded-plate assembly. A hand or hydraulic press brake handles box and pan work (trays, plinths, enclosures), while a slip roller forms cylinders and curves for organic forms. For sculpture, the roller is often the higher-value tool: curved steel sells.

Key parameters: minimum inside bend radius for mild steel is roughly 1Ã material thickness (air bending), and you must account for bend allowance when cutting blanks. For a 90Â° bend in 3 mm steel with a 6 mm punch and 50 mm die, expect a bend deduction of about 5 mm. Roller work requires multiple passes with decreasing radius â never try to achieve the final curve in one pass, or you will flatten the ends and oval the section.

Table 2: Bend allowance and roller pass guide (mild steel, 90Â° air bend)
ThicknessMin. inside radiusDie openingBend deductionRoller passes (to final radius)
1.5 mm1.5 mm12 mm~2.5 mm2â3
3 mm3 mm25 mm~5 mm3â4
5 mm5 mm40 mm~8 mm4â5
8 mm8 mm63 mm~13 mm5â7
10 mm10 mm80 mm~16 mm6â8

Source: TRUMPF, Bending Guide (trumpf.com); Amada, Bend Allowance Handbook (amada.co.jp). Values are indicative â verify against your tooling.

4. Advanced Welding: Vertical and Overhead

Most sculpture commissions require welding in position â a tall figure, a gate post, a canopy frame. Vertical-up (3G) and overhead (4G) are the positions that separate qualified fabricators from bench welders.

For SMAW (stick) on 3â6 mm steel: use 2.5â3.2 mm E6013 or E7018 electrodes, reduce amperage 10â15% versus flat, and use a slight upward drag for vertical-up. For overhead, keep the arc short, increase travel speed, and use a weave no wider than 2Ã electrode diameter. For MIG/MAG: drop voltage 1â2 V and wire speed slightly, and use a push angle of 5â15Â°. For TIG on thin sculpture work, vertical and overhead require lower amperage and faster travel to avoid sag.

Business note: clients pay a premium for on-site welding. A fabricator who can weld a 3 m gate frame in position without dismantling it can quote 20â30% more than one who must bring it back to the shop. Practise vertical and overhead until they are as reliable as flat.

5. Jigs and Fixtures for Repetition

If you make the same component more than three times â a leaf, a bracket, a base ring â build a jig. A jig is any device that holds parts in the correct position for welding or machining; a fixture is a jig that also clamps. In African sculpture workshops, simple angle-iron and toggle-clamp jigs cut assembly time by 40â70% and eliminate rework.

Design rules: locate from the part's functional surfaces, use quick-release clamps, allow for weld shrinkage (typically 1â2 mm per 100 mm of weld), and make the jig from material thicker than the workpiece so it does not distort. Copper or aluminium backing bars prevent weld sticking and act as heat sinks on thin sheet.

6. Project: Fabricated Steel Structure

Capstone project: design and build a freestanding sculptural steel structure â a 2.4 m tall abstract form in 6 mm plate and 40Ã40Ã3 mm square tube, with at least one rolled curve, one bolted connection, and one welded joint in vertical or overhead position. Deliverables: a cutting list, a bend schedule, a welding procedure (position, electrode, amperage), and a finish specification (wire brush + zinc-rich primer + topcoat, or patina).

Quote the job as if for a client: material, consumables, labour hours, transport, and a 20% margin. This is the business-first habit that turns a course certificate into income.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. PPE first: face shield, leather apron, gloves, ear plugs, steel-toe boots â before any tool is switched on.
  2. Check discs and electrodes: correct type, undamaged, within expiry, matched to material and thickness.
  3. Set the machine: amperage, gas flow, wire speed, or standoff verified against the material chart before the first cut or arc.
  4. Clamp the work: nothing moves during cutting, grinding, bending, or welding â no hand-held workpieces under a disc.
  5. Measure twice, cut once: mark, punch, and check the cutting list; account for kerf and bend deduction.
  6. Weld in position if the client needs it: vertical and overhead welds must be as clean as flat welds.
  7. Use the jig: if you are making it a fourth time, stop and build a fixture.
  8. Finish and inspect: dress welds, remove spatter, apply protective coating, and photograph the finished piece for your portfolio.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Hypertherm â Plasma Cutting Guide and Safety Manuals: hypertherm.com
  • ESAB â Plasma and Welding Handbooks (free PDFs): esab.com
  • Lincoln Electric â Welding Guide: Stick, MIG, TIG, Positions: lincolnelectric.com
  • 3M Abrasive Systems â Grinding and Cutting Safety Guide: 3m.com
  • Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) â Welding, Cutting and Brazing Standards (29 CFR 1910 Subpart Q): osha.gov

Adapted for rise AFRICA Skills â Metal Sculpture, Advanced Fabrication module. All links are free and maintained by the cited organisations. Verify local voltage, gas availability, and consumable supply before quoting a job in your market.

quiz.q: What is the recommended standoff distance between the plasma torch tip and the metal for a clean cut?
quiz.explanation: A standoff of 1.5â3mm maintains the arc while minimizing dross and tip damage.

quiz.q: Which gas is commonly used as the plasma gas in a plasma cutter?
quiz.explanation: Compressed air is the most common and cost-effective plasma gas for manual plasma cutting.

quiz.q: What should you do before piercing metal with a plasma cutter?
quiz.explanation: Tilting the torch 30Â° blows molten metal away from the tip, preventing damage.

quiz.q: What is dross in plasma cutting?
options: B) Recast metal on the bottom of the cut
quiz.explanation: Dross is molten metal that resolidifies on the underside of the cut, often due to incorrect speed or amperage.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential when plasma cutting?
options: B) Face shield with shade #8 or darker
quiz.explanation: A face shield with shade #8 or darker protects eyes from bright UV and infrared radiation.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness of steel a 40-amp plasma cutter can cleanly cut?
quiz.explanation: A 40-amp plasma cutter is typically rated for up to 10mm thick steel.

quiz.q: What is the correct disc to use for grinding?
quiz.explanation: Grinding discs are designed for side-loading and material removal, unlike cutting discs.

quiz.q: What is the maximum RPM for a 115mm angle grinder disc?
quiz.explanation: Most 115mm grinders run at 11,000 RPM, so discs must be rated at least that high.

quiz.q: What should you do if an angle grinder disc binds and kicks back?
options: B) Release the trigger and hold firmly
quiz.explanation: Releasing the trigger while holding firmly prevents the grinder from twisting out of your hands.

quiz.q: What is the correct angle to hold a grinder for general grinding?
quiz.explanation: A 15â30Â° angle prevents gouging and gives a smooth finish.

quiz.q: Why should you never use a cutting disc for grinding?
options: A) It wears out too fast
C) It creates too many sparks
quiz.explanation: Cutting discs are thin and not designed for side loads; they can shatter and cause injury.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a flap disc?
quiz.explanation: Flap discs are used for grinding, blending, and finishing metal surfaces.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a brake in metal fabrication?
quiz.explanation: A brake (press brake or box-and-pan brake) is used to make straight bends in sheet metal.

quiz.q: What is springback in bending?
options: A) The metal returning partially to its original shape
quiz.explanation: Springback is the elastic recovery of metal after bending, requiring overbending to achieve the desired angle.

quiz.q: How many rolls does a basic slip roller have?
quiz.explanation: A slip roller has three rolls: one top and two bottom, to form curves.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness a 1.2m manual brake can typically bend?
quiz.explanation: A 1.2m manual brake usually has a capacity of around 1.5mm mild steel.

quiz.q: What motion is recommended for vertical-up welding with 7018?
quiz.explanation: A triangle motion with pauses at the sides ensures good penetration and a clean bead in vertical-up welding.

quiz.q: Why is downhill welding generally weaker than uphill?
quiz.explanation: Downhill welding has less penetration because the arc tends to ride on top of the puddle.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for overhead welding with 3.2mm 7018?
quiz.explanation: Overhead welding requires slightly lower amperage (about 10â15% less than flat) to control the puddle.

quiz.q: What is the key to preventing molten metal from dripping in overhead welding?
options: B) Short arc and small puddle
quiz.explanation: A short arc and small puddle allow the metal to freeze quickly before dripping.

quiz.q: What type of electrode is commonly used for vertical-down welding on thin metal?
quiz.explanation: 6013 is a fast-freeze electrode suitable for vertical-down on thin sections.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a jig?
quiz.explanation: A jig holds the workpiece in a fixed position for repetitive operations.

quiz.q: What is a fixture?
options: A) A device that holds the tool
B) A device that holds the workpiece
quiz.explanation: A fixture holds the tool (e.g., a drill bushing) relative to the workpiece.

quiz.q: What material is commonly used to make jigs in African workshops?
quiz.explanation: Scrap steel is durable, weldable, and readily available in most workshops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance for locating pins in a jig?
quiz.explanation: 0.5mm clearance allows easy loading and unloading without excessive play.

quiz.q: Why is a copper backing bar used in welding jigs?
quiz.explanation: Copper conducts heat away quickly, reducing distortion and burn-through.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a fabricated steel structure?
quiz.explanation: A cut list ensures you have all pieces cut to the correct dimensions before assembly.

quiz.q: In the bench project, what is the purpose of the jig for leg assemblies?
options: B) To ensure identical leg positions
quiz.explanation: The jig holds the legs and rail in the correct position for consistent welding.

quiz.q: What welding position is used for the underside of the bench frame?
quiz.explanation: Welding on the underside of a structure requires overhead welding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for seat slats in the bench project?
quiz.explanation: A 10mm gap allows for drainage and expansion while providing comfort.
